title: Charismatic renewal (1967)
hook: a movement of praise and gifts of the Spirit that began at a student retreat

segments.voice: Yesterday, two forms of the Latin rite: one Roman Canon, prayed in both, and strong feelings on every side. Your line was one church, both loved. Did a sharp word become a question? Day one thousand four hundred five.

A weekend retreat house outside Pittsburgh. A group of college students from Duquesne University has come to pray, and they've been reading the opening chapters of the Acts of the Apostles, the ones about the wind and the fire at Pentecost. Their question is simple and a little dangerous: could that still happen? By the movement's own telling, on the Saturday night some of them wandered into the chapel, one by one, and didn't come out for a long time. They prayed, they praised, some of them wept, some laughed. Nobody had planned it. Out of that weekend, people say, a movement spread through the Catholic Church. Today, charismatic renewal.
screen: `A STUDENT RETREAT, READING ACTS.` → `COULD THAT STILL HAPPEN?` → `INTO THE CHAPEL, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: Start with the page those students were reading. At Pentecost, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and they began to speak with divers tongues, according as the Holy Ghost gave them to speak." The renewal takes that as more than a memory. Its members pray, in their own words, for the Spirit to stir up what was already given in baptism and confirmation. They call it being baptized in the Spirit, and they're careful to say it isn't a new sacrament. Next, the name. The movement takes it from charisms, the gifts of grace Paul writes about. Writing to Corinth, he lists them: wisdom, knowledge, healing, prophecy, tongues and more. And he insists, "Now there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit." The Catechism takes Paul's line: charisms are graces given for building up the Church, and they're to be received with gratitude and tested by the Church's pastors. Then, what it looks like. A prayer meeting in a parish hall. Songs of praise, some hands raised, a reading, a long stretch of people praising God aloud in their own words, sometimes praying in tongues, then quiet. For some Catholics this is home. Others pray in silence and find it strange. Both are in the same Church. Last, the guardrail Paul himself set for an enthusiastic church: "Let all things be done decently, and according to order." Praise, then, with the Church's order around it. One short line runs through its prayer meetings: come, Holy Spirit.
screen: `PENTECOST: FILLED WITH THE HOLY GHOST.` · `CHARISM: A GIFT OF GRACE.` · `A PRAYER MEETING IN A PARISH HALL.` · `DECENTLY, AND ACCORDING TO ORDER.` · then, large: `DIVERSITIES OF GRACES, BUT THE SAME SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray in praise for a minute. Settle, and breathe. Praise is different from asking and different from thanks. It's naming what someone is, not what they've done for you. If you pray, you can spend this sit praising God in your own plain words, out loud or silently, one name or one quality at a time, and you can begin the way the renewal does: come, Holy Spirit. If you don't, name, one by one, things that are good simply because they are: light, a voice you love, water. The bell holds the time.
Charismatic renewal. A Catholic movement of praise that asks the Holy Spirit to stir up the gifts of grace Paul called charisms. Today's word.

Your line: come, spirit. Today, at one moment when you feel flat or stuck, say those two words under your breath before you go on. And with today, our stretch on devotions closes. Day one thousand four hundred five.

howItsDone: Catholics in the charismatic renewal gather in prayer groups, often in parish halls, for songs of praise, scripture, spontaneous prayer and sometimes praying in tongues, and they pray for a renewal of the Holy Spirit's gifts first given in baptism and confirmation. Other Catholics take no part, and both are fully part of the Church.

notes: The origin story (a weekend retreat for Duquesne University students near Pittsburgh, reading Acts, students going into the chapel on the Saturday night) is attributed to 'the movement's own telling'. The index title's year 1967 is kept in the title only. Confirm the details.
Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 2:4, 1 Corinthians 12:4 and 14:40 ('But let all things...' — leading 'But' dropped): confirm.

'Baptism in the Spirit' explained as the renewal's own term, 'not a new sacrament', a release or stirring up of baptismal and confirmation grace. Confirm the phrasing is fair to the renewal and to the Church's teaching.
CCC 799–801 (charisms for building up the Church; discernment by pastors): paraphrased; confirm.
'Come, Holy Spirit' described as a line that 'runs through its prayer meetings': confirm; no specific prayer text is quoted.
The practice invites praise 'in your own plain words'; no new prayer text is written.
